title: Thin Protocol, ToolCall Hedging, and SDK Edges — PRD Notes
content:
Context:
This doc collects a compact set of proposals for a low-footprint streaming protocol ("thin protocol") optimized for mobile/edge clients, hedging semantics for tool calls to improve latency/availability, and small but opinionated SDK ergonomics to make progressive delivery and structured output easier to adopt.

Why now:
- Increasing demand from mobile-first customers who need partial responses and predictable tail latency.
- Tool-calling adoption is accelerating — we need clearer contract semantics for retries/hedging and deterministic structured outputs.
- Current SDK surfaces are inconsistent across languages; many apps implement fragile workarounds for backpressure and resumed streams.

Goals:
- Define a minimal wire protocol extension for streaming partial structured frames and lightweight tool-call markers.
- Specify hedging semantics for tool invocations so clients and server can race tool backends without duplicating side-effects.
- Propose SDK ergonomics (JS + Python) that make partial JSON assembly, error semantics, and resume logic straightforward.
- Ensure observability hooks: token-level tracing, tool-call provenance, and client-visible fallback reasons.

Non-goals:
- Full serialization format overhaul (we keep JSON frames).
- Solving arbitrary at-most-once semantics for every third-party tool — we'll provide primitives and recommended patterns.

Success metrics (90 days):
- 80% of streaming client codepaths use the new SDK helper rather than homegrown parsers.
- 25% reduction in median perceived latency for mobile median-TTFP on sample apps.
- <1% increase in accidental duplicate external tool side-effects in canary for hedging-enabled routes.

Design principles / constraints:
- Minimal parsing overhead on small devices: frames should be self-contained and delimiting simple.
- Backward-compatible with existing streaming endpoints: old clients should continue receiving text streams.
- Explicit surface for partial-structured output (not heuristics over text).
- Hedging should be opt-in at route or call time; autopolicy for safe idempotent tool calls.

Protocol sketch (wire-level, high level):
- Transport: existing HTTP/2 or websockets for streaming; keep server-sent events (SSE) option.
- Frame envelope: simple JSON lines where each line is a frame object with a small set of required fields. Example frame (one line):
  {"t":"frame","id":"f_1","type":"partial","payload":"{\"items\":[...]}"}
- Required frame fields: t (frame type), id (frame id), seq (optional sequence number), route (call route id), ts (iso timestamp). Keep id to allow dedup/resume.
- Frame types we define: 
  - handshake: initial meta (schema, session id, version).
  - partial: partial structured chunk (may contain "schema_cursor" to indicate JSON path chunked).
  - text: raw string chunks (backcompat).
  - tool_call: announces a tool invocation about to start or in-flight with metadata and an invocation id.
  - tool_result: structured tool result; includes invocation id and optional guarantee flag.
  - ack / backpressure: server -> client signals about batching/backoff preferences.
  - error: terminal error frame with machine-readable code and human message.

Partial structured frames:
- We intentionally allow partial JSON "slices" mapped to logical paths to avoid reserializing huge objects on-device. Eg: payload carries a base64 or escaped chunk for path "/choices/0" and schema_cursor indicates where to stitch.
- SDKs provide a composer that knows how to assemble partial frames into a final JSON object; if assembly fails, SDK surfaces a "partial-result" error with what was assembled.

Tool-call hedging semantics (server-side + client API):
- Hedging goal: reduce tail latency by issuing multiple in-flight tool requests to different tool backends when latency SLOs are at risk, but avoid duplicate side effects.
- Invocation model:
  - Client marks tool as hedgable and provides an idempotency token and side-effect-safety hint (safe-read, idempotent-write, non-idempotent).
  - Server binary will only hedge if tool is tagged as hedgable and mode allows (route config).
  - When hedging, server ensures single-commit strategy: tool backends are requested in parallel but only one result is used for downstream; for non-idempotent writes, server must use a coordinator or an external transaction system (e.g., task queue dedupe).
- Tool frames: tool_call frame sent before invoking, includes invocation_id, tool_name, input_digest (hash), idempotency_token, hedging_allowed boolean.
- tool_result frame includes invocation_id, result, source_backend_id, commit_strategy (used/ignored).
- Recommended defaults: read-only tools -> hedging allowed; write tools -> hedging disabled unless external dedupe provided.

SDK ergonomics (JS + Python patterns):
- Provide an incremental "Composer" API that returns an async iterator over assembled partial results and exposes progress events.
- Example (JS pseudo):
  const stream = client.hosted.stream({model, prompt, toolHints});
  for await (const frame of stream.composed()) {
    if (frame.type === 'partial') renderPartial(frame.path, frame.value);
    if (frame.type === 'tool_call') showToolPending(frame.tool_name);
    if (frame.type === 'tool_result') applyToolResult(frame.invocation_id, frame.result);
  }
- Backpressure handling: SDK exposes `stream.requestMore(n)` and `stream.pause()` to allow apps to defer processing or throttle network reception on resource-limited devices.
- Resume behavior: SDK persists last-seen frame id; on reconnect, client requests resume with last_id and server streams missing frames (idempotent resume).
- Error mapping: provide deterministic codes (STREAM_TRUNCATED, TOOL_FAILED, SCHEMA_MISMATCH) and guidance on when to retry vs. surface to user.

Observability / telemetry:
- Each frame tagged with route, call_id, frame_id, and optionally token_counts.
- Tool-call frames record backend latency, hedging attempts, and commit decision.
- SDKs emit high-level events out to console/metrics: partial_assembly_time, resume_success, hedged_tool_count.

Rollout & migration plan:
- Phase 0 (canary): implement protocol on a new experimental route /v1/stream-thin. Provide JS SDK alpha.
- Phase 1 (opt-in): allow existing streaming routes to enable thin-frames via query param or header. Collect telemetry for assembly success and hedging duplicates.
- Phase 2 (surface): promote to GA when assembly success >99% across clients and duplicate side-effect rate <0.5% for hedged routes.

Compatibility & fallback:
- Old clients: if a client doesn't understand frame types, server will emit text frames in addition to structured frames until client signals new handshake version.
- Mobile fallback: SDK default is low-memory mode where we limit in-memory partial assembly and write intermediate artifacts to temporary file.

Security considerations:
- Tool-call hedging increases surface for accidental duplicate-sensitive effects; require explicit tool metadata and server policy gating for hedging.
- Frames may contain PII in tool payloads; require route-level encryption at rest and selective redaction for telemetry.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Should we standardize a small binary framing (msgpack) for further size reduction? Pros: smaller, faster parse; Cons: more brittle for debugging and not human-readable.
- How to coordinate hedging across multi-region (avoid cross-region double-exec)? Options: global coordinator vs. region-local plus regional dedupe tokens.
- Is it worth adding a single-pass incremental JSONPath expression language for schema_cursor?
- UX: what do SDKs do when schema mismatch is partial? Provide heuristic merges or fail fast?

Implementation notes (engineering):
- Serving runtime: add a serializer module that can emit frame-lines with stable ids and sequence hints. Hook into existing prefix caching to avoid retransmitting unchanged parts.
- Router: add hedging policy flags and tool metadata propagation. Ensure canary routes cannot enable hedging for write tools by default.
- Console: add telemetry dashboards for hedged tool invocations and duplicate side-effects, plus per-route assembly success metric.

Appendix: Quick dev checklist
- [ ] Prototype JS Composer with resume & backpressure (2 engineers, 3 weeks)
- [ ] Wire-format RFC and sample SSE/http2 lines (docs + examples)
- [ ] Server serializer + router hedging flag (infra + serving-runtime)
- [ ] Canary integration test: synthetic tool with toggleable idempotency to measure duplicates
- [ ] Observability: add logs/traces for frames and tool commit decisions

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally compact; the goal is to give a runnable experiment that teams can opt into quickly. Please flag any scenarios we miss (esp. enterprise compliance concerns around tool payloads).
- If you want a narrower scope for Phase 0, we can split out hedging to a follow-up RFC and land thin partial frames + SDK composer first.

End of doc.
